parts.transcript:
You will hear a phone conversation between a new employee and a pharmacy receptionist.
Receptionist: Good morning, this is Greenfield Pharmacy. How can I assist you?
Employee: Hi, I'm calling to check some details before I start my new job there. I was given a few notes, but I just want to confirm them.
Receptionist: Of course. Our manager, John Field, is available if you need further clarification.
Employee: Great. I also need to save the pharmacy's contact number. Can you tell me?
Receptionist: Certainly. It's 0491570159.
Employee: Got it. Now, regarding my shifts, I was told that I start quite early in the morning.
Receptionist: Yes, most of our employees begin their shifts before the store opens. Your shift starts at 7.45 a.m. That way, you'll have time to prepare for the first customers.
Employee: All right. I also heard there's one late-night opening each week.
Receptionist: That's correct. The store stays open late on Friday evenings. It's usually our busiest night, so we need all hands on deck.
Employee: Good to know. And my official start date?
Receptionist: You'll be starting from the 22nd of January, so be sure to arrive a little early on your first day to complete any remaining paperwork.
Employee: Thanks. Also, I remember something about uniforms. Should I bring my own?
Receptionist: No, that won't be necessary. We provide staff with a uniform, and Barbara will assist you in getting the right size.
Employee: All right, and I believe John is going to email me about another matter.
Receptionist: Yes, he'll send you some details about parking, including where you can leave your vehicle and the spaces allocated for staff members.
Employee: Perfect. Now, about the facilities. I recall there's a machine available for customers to use, right?
Receptionist: Yes, we have a weight machine near the entrance. Customers often use it to check their body weight. Just ensure that it's functioning properly at all times.
Employee: Will do. If a customer needs medical assistance, who should they speak to?
Receptionist: We always have a nurse on duty so they can approach the counter and ask for help if necessary.
Employee: Got it. And I should be careful when lifting heavy stock, right?
Receptionist: Absolutely. We store some large boxes at the back and if they aren't lifted correctly, you might injure your back. So, make sure to bend your knees and avoid straining yourself.
Employee: That makes sense. Oh, one last thing. I heard that the store has introduced new bags. What do they look like?
Receptionist: Yes, we've recently switched to a more eco-friendly option. They now come in purple, so they're easy to spot.
Employee: That's helpful. Thanks for all the information.

parts.transcript:
You will hear a recorded audio guide for visitors to the State Museum.
Welcome to the State Museum, situated in the centre of this truly multicultural metropolis which is home to more than 30 different nationalities. The museum has a number of exciting displays and exhibitions, and this audio guide is designed to help you fully enjoy your visit. There are 15 galleries in total, and this season sees the opening of three new exhibitions. We suggest that you start your tour with these highlights of the season.
The Heritage Clothes Exhibition is located in Gallery 3 of the museum. People who live in the area have spent two years preparing this exhibition, which brings together some of the fascinating garments traditionally worn in their own communities. The photos that accompany each exhibit were taken by some of the city's college students, who are studying design and show the clothes being modelled by the real people who wear them in the course of their everyday lives.
Another remarkable highlight of the season is the exhibition known as Toys from the Past, which can be visited in Gallery 9. This exhibition, appealing to people of all ages, is on tour throughout the country and will be here for ten weeks only. The gigantic board games laid out on the gallery floor are among the most popular activities in the exhibition and should not be missed. A special display of miniature toys brings this exhibition to an end. These small objects are on loan from countries all over the world.
The final highlight of the season is the Biscuit Gallery, number 15. The factory manufactured round, square, triangular and hexagonal tins for a whole range of different occasions. When the factory finally closed, it announced that people's favourite biscuit was a plain, savoury one which was eaten with cheese. When you get to the end of the exhibition, there is an entertaining, hands-on activity to fill your own biscuit tin.
If you would like to buy a memento of your visit, there is a museum gift shop which sells postcards, souvenirs and handmade pottery next to the information desk on the ground floor. And finally, if you don't want to carry your coats and bags around with you during your visit, please make use of the complimentary lockers provided by the museum. Enjoy your visit!

parts.transcript:
You will hear two university students, Jen and Rob, discussing their forensic linguistics project.
Jen: Hi, Rob.
Rob: Hi, Jen. We need to look at this project we're doing together in forensic linguistics.
Jen: Sure. I'm glad we chose voice identification as the topic.
Rob: Yeah, we've been given a voice recording of a possible suspect. We've got to listen to the recording and analyse their voice.
Jen: Well, I've already listened to the recording, and I can't even tell if it's a man or a woman. But where we're really going to get in trouble is that the recording is very unclear. I'm sure they've done that to test us.
Rob: Well, they weren't going to make it easy. And then we have to interview the suspect and make our own recording face-to-face and decide if it's the same person as on the original recording.
Jen: Yes. But they might do something like speaking with another accent because the tutor suggests they do that just to test us.
Rob: So let's get on with it then. Oh, and don't start your usual self-doubt about whether you can do the work or not. You usually do OK in the end. I reckon that as long as we focus on the main points of the assignment, we can think about the finer details later.
Jen: We'll have to do some background reading first. I'll go to the library later and get what we need.
Rob: OK. I've already looked at forensics today and it didn't say much about voice identification, so we needn't bother with that one. Research methods in forensic linguistics — I guess we ought to borrow that. And voice identification will be a useful one — I'll borrow that from our classmate George. But we should get out Modern Forensic Techniques. We need all the help we can get on that subject.
Jen: OK, that's that sorted out. Now on to the practical stuff. I'm not sure about how we're going to record the voices. I'm not too good on the technical side.
Rob: Me neither. We'd better work out what we're doing. I'm more worried about fitting in the writing up.
Jen: I know. We've got loads of other assignments to finish as well. Now, Rob, let's decide how we're going to split the writing between us. Are you any good at introductions?
Rob: They always seem to let me down.
Jen: OK, leave that to me. Are you OK to do the literature review, then?
Rob: Maybe we should split that part. I don't mind writing the methodology section if you feel comfortable doing the discussion and conclusions.
Jen: OK. And we can do the analysis between us as well.

parts.transcript:
You will hear a university lecture about the salamander.
Salamander is a fascinating amphibian that is often mistaken for a lizard due to its elongated body, short legs and tail. However, unlike reptiles, salamanders have moist, permeable skin which they rely on for respiration. One of the most distinctive features of many salamanders is their spots, which serve as a form of camouflage or warning to potential predators. Some species have bright coloration, signaling their toxicity, while others blend into their surroundings to avoid detection.
Salamanders possess an extraordinary ability: they can regenerate their limbs, and even parts of their spinal cord. And remarkably, they can also regenerate their heart. This makes them a subject of interest in scientific research, particularly in the field of regenerative medicine. Their diet consists of small insects, worms and other invertebrates, often found in damp environments where leaves accumulate on the forest floor. These areas provide both shelter and food sources for these amphibians.
Salamanders also play a critical role in the carbon cycle. By consuming leaf litter insects, they indirectly help regulate carbon levels in ecosystems, preventing excess decomposition that releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. However, their survival is heavily dependent on the health of their habitat, particularly the soil, where they lay eggs and seek refuge. Contaminated soil can have devastating effects on their populations.
One of the biggest threats to salamanders today is environmental pollution. Chemicals from agricultural runoff, industrial waste, and even road salt seep into their habitats, causing declines in many species. Despite these challenges, salamanders have long been valued in traditional medicine. Some cultures believe that their secretions have healing properties, though modern science has yet to fully verify these claims.
Interestingly, salamanders are sometimes confused with a frog, especially in their larval stage, when they have external gills similar to those of tadpoles. Finally, temperature plays a crucial role in their survival. Since they rely on external sources of heat, fluctuations in temperature due to climate change pose a significant threat to their populations, affecting their breeding patterns and metabolic rates.
